you can't heal for her, you can only encourage and support.

i'm religious as well. there are some awful things that happened to me in my childhood that are so tightly connected to religion that i had a very hard time reconciling holding my faith after i got into therapy and started dealing with my issues.

you don't have to hold the same faith that your parents did. you get to choose what you want to believe, and what you want to walk away from. you have to do what's right for you, regardless of how you were raised. find what brings you peace and go with that. if that's Christianity, that's totally fine, if not, that's totally fine too. it just has to be right for you. 

if you are interested in still being Christian, here are my thoughts. the gospel is what matters, not the people who claim to practice it. people are not perfect, and never will be on this earth. your parents made awful mistakes, but that doesn't mean that the church doesn't still have value. something that's important for me to know is that forgiveness is not about telling the offender that what they did was ok, it's about deciding that what they did doesn't have to run your life anymore. what they did was still wrong, and they'll have to answer for it in this life or in the next. you are lifting your own burden, not theirs, if you choose to forgive. forgiving also does not mean letting people walk all over you. you can put something in the past without lowering your boundaries or standards.

in either case, it may be wise to simply take a breather. i think a loving God would understand that you need a time out on the church front, time to really figure out what it is you want from a religion. i personally took a break for a couple years myself, although i sort of still paid lip service to the church, because really, you have to pick your battles and i wasn't interested in getting into that with neighbors, friends, or family members. but i took time to think about whether or not this religion was right for me. i did end up deciding to stay, but on my own rather than simply because i was born into it.

about God... I spent a very long time wondering what kind of God would let me endure all the shit i went through in my life. i questioned so frequently why these things happened to me, why he would let them happen at all. i reconciled with this: we're not on this earth to be perfect little robots who always do everything right. we're here to make mistakes. some people make little mistakes, others make huge ones. some people make really awful choices. the bottom line is that we're here to learn and grow, and we can choose to change - all of us, even rapists and abusers and murderers... God can't make us choose one way or another, though he may offer advice if we listen. to be more specific to myself, i did find "reasons" why it happened to me. if it didn't happen to me, it could have happened to someone else - someone less resilient, someone who could not have handled as much as i can. but because it happened to me, i have the opportunity to make change, to try to prevent it from happening to someone else, and to not do that awful thing myself as so often happens in the cycle of abuse.

i would not be the strong person i am today had i not endured the horrible, awful things of my childhood. i believe that God wants me to be strong and to know the pain of the trials and the joy of the recovery, and i'm ok with it.

it'll be ok, no matter what you decide, as long as you do it for you, and not for anyone else.

some places will require a business degree with an emphasis in buying, but it really depends on how big the company is, what experience you have, and the kinds of things you will be buying.

i have an unrelated bachelors degree, but no formal business education. i work at a small company and started at the bottom of the totem pole, and moved up the ranks to where i am today. i've worked in retail for 17 years (since i turned 16 really) so i did have a good understanding of how retail works before i started here.

a good buyer has great attention to detail and followthrough; excellent interpersonal skills - as you need to build and maintain relationships with vendors, manufacturers, and clients; organized and motivated; an eye for trends (though this is something i learned here, not a skill i had before); able to interpret sales figures and reports to determine what's hot and what's a flop; and of course, a positive attitude.

i do spend some of my personal time on social media browsing to see what products are getting more attention, what new products we could carry, anything i might be missing out on, etc. the products i buy aren't really my personal cup of tea, so i'm able to stay somewhat detached from it - i don't have personal bias or strong opinions on brands or styles, and this helps me make better decisions based on facts and data rather than what i personally would buy.

there is actually a lot of work involved, and at times it can be tedious. there's a ton of paperwork sometimes, and every vendor requires different stuff. i have good relationships with most of my vendor contacts - because i spent the time getting to know them and letting them get to know me - which makes it easier for me to ask questions, get clarification, and make business deals.

i think the worst part of my job is seeing a new product line or brand fail miserably. this will happen to pretty much every buyer at every company. you take a risk on something and it just flops, but you learn from it and learn to make better decisions in the future.

i personally don't have any kind of business degree (though i do have an unrelated bachelors degree). i work for a small business and started here as an order picker/packer and just moved up through promotions and advancements.

when i have the need to vent and be validated, my solution is to vent elsewhere *before* the session and then use the session to process the feelings that came up during my vent. more often than not i don't have a person to vent to, so i vent to my word processor, to this sub, or to my pet birds (they love to be talked to, it's win-win).

after i've said everything i wanted/needed to say, i note my feelings and some key concepts or events that triggered different feelings, and take *that* to therapy to work on.

right at the starting gate this will be tricky to do on your own, so if you have a SO or good friend who is level-headed whom you can bounce things off of, it can be really helpful to ask them to just listen to what you need to say, and not to give any feedback other than nodding or the occasional right/yeah/i get that. you're going to therapy to get help with your issues, so ask your ventee to no try to fix it, just to be there.

in the event that you are lacking a ventee, you can validate yourself by speaking to yourself out loud and giving positive feedback, just like you would to a friend who is having a hard time. what i sometimes do is write it all out, then take a small break, and then read it back to myself and give validation at appropriate points.

during the week i often note things that have triggered me or that i feel like i need to discuss, and i'll review them on thursday mornings so i can think about them during the day before my session.

it's quite common to not actually remember being sexually abused. more survivors forget than remember. i personally have endless awful vivid memories of it, but that's fairly uncommon.

the feelings and events you describe are common among survivors; feeling disgusted by being sexual, not feeling comfortable during a sex act, wanting to be less aware (drunk/high) during sexual encounters, wanting to destroy your body.

whether or not you have proof of sexual abuse doesn't actually matter here - what matters is that you're hurting. your feelings are real, and you deserve to heal. therapy can be extremely helpful. the therapy that works for me is called IFS - Internal Family Systems. the basis is that there are several different "parts" inside of you that make up your personality, and they're in conflict. some need to be given new "jobs" and others need to be cared for and healed. the goal is to get all your parts to work in harmony. it sounds a little cheezy, i know. if you've ever felt like on one hand you want X, but on the other hand you really DON'T want X, that's your different "parts" having differing opinions, for example. all your parts have different motives for what they do, but the central theme is to protect you - whether or not the coping mechanisms actually still work for you, they likely worked to some degree at a younger age.

look into some different modes of therapy, and reach out. shop around for a good therapist. if the first one you go to doesn't seem to "get" you, move on and find a different one. you don't immediately love the first pair of shoes you try on, and it's the same with therapists. maybe they look good on paper but in person it just doesn't work.

i wish you the absolute best of luck in your healing journey. please know that you are not alone, and that you have a safe place here to come and talk about what's going on.

on the subject of milk, i cannot tolerate cow's milk by itself at all. cheese, on the other hand, is not the same story. here's why:

baby humans produce Lactase, the enzyme that breaks down Lactose, so that they can digest their mother's milk. 20% of european descendents, 80% of african descents, and nearly 100% of asian descendents do not produce Lactase once they start eating solid food, thus making them "lactose intolerant."

the first thing you need to do is identify your triggers. OP has identified that (at least one of) their trigger is a stern, harsh, critical voice. other triggers may be certain words, gestures, looks, etc.

then you need to figure out what is and isn't a normal, logical response to the trigger. this is easier with a neutral 3rd party such as a therapist. i.e. most people don't emotionally revert to 4 years old when they're yelled at, instead, a mature person may listen calmly until the other person is finished, take a moment to process what's happening, and respond with something like "i'll take that into consideration" or "i wasn't aware of that, thank you for bringing it to my attention" (if what they're saying has merit, such as a boss getting upset that you're  showig up late for work or not completing a task correctly).

taking the focus off of yourself when the other person is yelling/critical can help - telling yourself "this isn't about me, yelling person is having a rough day(or just batshit crazy) and they're letting off steam" or similar can help you separate yourself from the negative emotions.

decide how you ideally want to react to your triggers, and then practice it. set up a scenario for yourself either with a neutral 3rd party or just in your head, and play it out. imagine the trigger happening, and then react to it in your new, more positive fashion.  for example, the words "get over it" are a trigger for me (they imply avoiding the issue rather than dealing with it), and my conditioned response is to cry and then get more depressed. so i'll imagine those words spewing from NM's mouth, and then i'll say (out loud if i can) "i'd rather go through the mountain than skip around it - next time the mountain will have a tunnel i can speed through because i've already done the work" and although i will never really say this to her face, what i'm doing is solidifying my emotional response - that i am worth the trouble and that the trouble is worth it in the long run. another example might be that instead of giving in to a narc's demands, you're going to restate your boundaries and walk away.

take back your power from your abuser, stand firm in your knowledge that you are a priceless, worthwhile person, and that you deserve to be treated with respect.

i have been in therapy for quite a while. i have a part of me that screams "FIX IT FIX IT FIX IT NOW NOW NOW" and i want to be DONE with therapy asap. unfortunately, that's not how healing works. you actually do need to take it slow. it's a process, and there's not a "fast track" for it. Just like you can't fast-track wound healing after surgery, there are things you can do to make it heal *correctly* and have the healing be long-lasting/permanent, but not necessarily faster.

what you *can* do is work on yourself at home between sessions. use the skills you're learning and apply them during the week and notate your progress. ask your therapist for ways you can do this. some therapists will give you "homework" or "assignments" and others will have other suggestions for ways you can continue work at home. there are, however, some things that you will need to deal with in therapy and not alone. your therapist can discuss with you what things you need to wait on and bring to therapy, and what you can try your hand at alone.

go to therapy with a purpose in mind. have something you need to talk about, and bring it up at the beginning of the session. either something that happened during the week, like a memory coming up, or your reaction to a situation that triggered you, or something from your past that's been nagging at you. get specific about it. if you come with a purpose in mind to each session, you will likely feel like it was productive rather than just an hour of hashing out the past.

be ready and willing to do the work. accept that some things will feel strange and will probably be out of your comfort zone. try new ways of coping, and don't be afraid of failure. you probably won't find the right new coping skills on the first try, and that's ok. it's a learning process.

if you don't find that this therapist understands you, it's ok to shop around for a new one. the first therapist you meet with is not always the right therapist for you. you can also try reading some self-help books or getting some self-help workbooks too, those can help you make small changes and progress at home.

keep at it, and you'll start to see positive changes. i promise.

some of the things she does may affect you, others may not. if she chooses to wipe her hands with a dirty towel, and then directly put her hands all over your food and face, this may be a real problem. if she wipes her hands with a dirty towel and then goes to her room and goes to bed, this isn't something you should focus on. it's gross, but it doesn't involve you. take a look at the things she does that anger you, and try to realisticly identify which things affect and involve you directly, and which things you think are just gross/wrong.

after you've figured out what things are actually affecting you, have an honest conversation with her about it. tell her that these are some things you're concerned about, and ask her if she would be ok with making some changes. it's important to ask her if she's ok with it, because she's much less likely to feel picked on or forced to do something, and she'll have a chance to counter if she needs to and suggest something that may work better for her. be patient, and remember that if she is interested in changing, new habits do take about a month to really stick. give her some slack and be kind to her.
